bionomics.survival_stage: Cyst in soil (dead female body containing eggs)
bionomics.egg_stage: Eggs remain protected inside cyst during unfavourable season

larval_stage.hatching: Eggs hatch inside cyst when conditions become favourable
larval_stage.entry_point: Larvae enter susceptible plants near root tips
larval_stage.movement: Larvae move through cortex and settle parallel to main root axis with head away from root tip

male_development.growth: Male increases in girth up to one-fifth of body length
male_development.body_form: Elongated and coiled within cuticle during third stage
male_development.adult_stage: After fourth moult, becomes cylindrical adult male

female_development.growth: Continues to increase in girth after second and third moults
female_development.final_moult: Fourth moult produces full-grown adult female
female_development.cyst_formation: After mating, eggs mature inside body; female dies and body converts into cyst

cultural_control: Crop rotation with non-host crops like mustard, pulses, fenugreek or carrot for one to two years
Plough the field two to three times during summer to expose cysts

pests.distribution_and_status: Cosmopolitan. Causes ear-cockle or mamni disease of wheat. Acts as a carrier of bacterial yellow slime ear-rot (Tundu disease) caused by Corynebacterium tritici.
damage_symptoms: Formation of black, rounded galls (mamni) in place of grains
When galls are soaked in water, the coat softens and large numbers of larvae are released
Affected plants are stunted
Leaves become wrinkled, rolled or twisted
Variable number of grains in an ear converted into galls
Diseased ears are shorter and thicker than healthy ears
Glumes are spread farther apart compared to healthy ears

bionomics.survival_stage: Dormant second-stage larvae inside dry galls
bionomics.gall_viability: Dry galls remain viable for long periods
bionomics.larval_activation: Larvae revive and become active when galls absorb moisture

larval_migration.release: Larvae released into soil when galls soften after sowing
larval_migration.movement_range: Larvae can reach host plants within one-third of a metre
larval_migration.feeding_site: Free parasites on young leaves and growing points

bionomics.flower_invasion: Larvae enter flower bud primordia during ear formation and induce gall formation instead of normal grains

sexual_development.population: About 40 females and 40 males per gall
sexual_development.reproduction: Mating occurs inside gall; females lay large numbers of eggs

bionomics.dormancy: Larvae develop up to second stage and become dormant in dry galls

physical_control: Separate galls from wheat seed by floating seed in water
Skim off floating galls (lighter than seeds)
Dry the cleaned seed thoroughly before sowing
cultural_control: Use clean, gall-free seed for sowing
One year fallowing is sufficient to eradicate the nematode from the field
